title: Hybrid locks
sub: Monitor inside out, Wait/Pulse, the Lock type in .NET 9 and the Slim family
cards/0/title: The best of spinning and of the kernel
cards/0/body:
Pure spinning burns the CPU, a kernel object is expensive even without contention. A hybrid lock takes the best of both and goes through three stages:

  • the fast path: the lock is free — one atomic CompareExchange and you are in. No kernel, no allocations, tens of nanoseconds;
  • a short spin: the lock is taken — spin a little, maybe the owner is about to leave;
  • sleep: did not make it — sleep on a kernel object until the owner wakes you on exit.

That is how lock (Monitor), the new Lock, SemaphoreSlim, ManualResetEventSlim and ReaderWriterLockSlim work. The Slim suffix means exactly this: a lightweight hybrid version with no kernel handle on the fast path.

The woken thread does not inherit the lock: it tries to take it again with the same CAS and may lose to a thread that has just arrived. That way the lock does not sit idle while the sleeper wakes up.
cards/1/body:
Where does lock (obj) keep its state? In the object header — the word in front of the type pointer. While there is no contention it holds a "thin lock": the owner thread's id and a recursion count. Taking it is one CAS on the header.

When a second thread finds the lock taken, it spins a little. If that does not help, the lock inflates: the CLR creates a sync block for the object — an entry in a separate table with a queue of waiters and a kernel event to sleep on. The sync block index is written into the header.

You know from the pitfalls unit that lock is Monitor.Enter plus Monitor.Exit in finally. But the shape of the call has changed. Before C# 4 the compiler put Monitor.Enter(obj) before try. In .NET Framework an asynchronous exception could arrive between returning from Enter and entering try — one thrown into the thread not by its own code but by someone outside. The main example is ThreadAbortException: another thread called Thread.Abort(), and the exception appeared at any point. The lock is already taken, but finally does not guard it yet: the lock stays taken forever, and everyone who comes for it hangs.

Since C# 4 Enter sits inside try and reports through ref bool lockTaken whether it managed to take the lock. Whatever happens, finally knows whether to release. Modern .NET does not support Thread.Abort (it throws PlatformNotSupportedException), but the shape stayed: it costs nothing and closes the gap between acquiring and try.
cards/1/deep:
The header is small, and the thin lock shares it with the default hash code. If the non-overridden GetHashCode was already called on the object, the hash sits in the header and lock goes straight through a sync block — and vice versa. That is why sync blocks exist at all: they hold whatever did not fit — the hash, the lock, COM interop data.

A sync block lives as long as the object. Hence the advice to lock on a dedicated private object: foreign code that does lock on your this or on typeof(...) shares the very same lock with you.
cards/2/q: Why does Monitor.Enter take a ref bool lockTaken parameter, when people used to write just Monitor.Enter(obj) before try?
cards/2/options/0: An exception could hit between taking the lock and entering try, and the lock would stay taken forever
cards/2/options/1: So that Enter can return false on a timeout
cards/2/options/3: So that the JIT does not hoist Enter out of a loop
cards/2/explain: In .NET Framework an asynchronous exception (ThreadAbortException) could arrive between Enter and try. The lock is taken, and finally never runs. With lockTaken, Enter itself is inside try, and finally knows for sure whether to release. Timeouts and reentrancy have nothing to do with it: Monitor is reentrant anyway.
cards/3/title: Wait and Pulse: waiting for a condition under a lock
cards/3/body:
Monitor is not just a lock but also a condition variable. A thread under the lock sees it is too early to continue (the queue is empty) and calls Monitor.Wait. That atomically releases the lock and puts the thread to sleep in the object's waiting queue.

Another thread takes the lock, changes the state and calls Pulse — moving one waiter to the ready queue (PulseAll moves all). The woken thread re-acquires the lock and only then returns from Wait.

Both methods may be called only while holding the lock on that object, otherwise you get SynchronizationLockException.

Important: Pulse does not hand the lock to the woken thread. It moves to the ready queue, waits until the producer leaves the lock, and then competes for the lock with everyone else. A third thread coming "from the street" may get in first and take the item. That is why the condition after Wait is always re-checked in a while loop, not once in an if.
cards/4/q: Put the events in order: a consumer waits, a producer adds an item
cards/4/items/0: The consumer takes the lock and sees an empty queue
cards/4/items/1: Wait releases the lock, the consumer falls asleep
cards/4/items/2: The producer takes the lock and adds an item
cards/4/items/3: Pulse moves the consumer to the ready queue
cards/4/items/5: The consumer re-acquires the lock and re-checks the condition
cards/4/explain: Pulse does not hand over the lock by itself: the consumer really wakes only when the producer leaves the lock. And between these moments a third thread can grab the lock.
cards/5/q: Two consumers. Sometimes Dequeue throws InvalidOperationException: the queue is empty. Which line is to blame?
cards/5/explain: Between Pulse and re-acquiring the lock, the second consumer can walk into the lock "from the street" and take the item. The first one wakes up, no longer checks the condition and reaches into an empty queue. The condition after Wait is always re-checked in a while loop.
cards/6/body:
You already saw a deadlock in the context and deadlock unit: the UI thread waits for a task, and the task waits for the UI thread. With locks it is just as easy — two threads take two locks in a different order:

1) thread 1 took _a; 2) thread 2 took _b; 3) thread 1 wants _b and waits: thread 2 holds it; 4) thread 2 wants _a and waits: thread 1 holds it.

Neither releases its lock until it gets the second one. No exception, the CPU is idle — two threads stand in Monitor.Enter forever.

How to stay out of it:

  • one order of acquiring across the whole program: always _a first, then _b. For objects of the same kind (two accounts) the order comes from a key, for example the Id;
  • do not call foreign code under a lock: an event, a callback or a virtual method may take its own locks in an order you do not know;
  • for diagnostics — Monitor.TryEnter(obj, timeout): it returns false if the lock was not taken in time, and you can log who is waiting for whom.
cards/7/q: A money transfer takes lock(from), then lock(to). Transfers A→B and B→A run at the same time. What can happen and how do you fix it?
cards/7/options/0: A deadlock; take the locks in account Id order, not in from/to order
cards/7/options/3: A deadlock; volatile on the Balance field will help
cards/7/explain: The A→B transfer holds A and waits for B, the B→A transfer holds B and waits for A. If you always take the account with the smaller Id first — var (first, second) = from.Id < to.Id ? (from, to) : (to, from); — both transfers start with the same account, and the second one simply waits for the first to finish.
cards/7/wrong/1: Reentrancy is about the same thread entering again. Here two different threads each hold a lock and wait for the other's.
cards/7/wrong/3: volatile is about the visibility of a field, not about the order of taking locks.
cards/8/body:
Since .NET 9 and C# 13 there is a dedicated System.Threading.Lock type. The lock state lives in the fields of the Lock object itself, not in the header of an arbitrary object and not in the sync block table. The docs recommend it for new locks as the fastest option.

The compiler recognizes the type: lock on a Lock becomes not Monitor.Enter but using (_gate.EnterScope()). EnterScope returns a ref struct whose Dispose releases the lock.

The catch: cast the Lock to object — and lock silently becomes the old header-based Monitor. The compiler warns: CS9216. And Lock has no Wait/Pulse: for condition variables you still need Monitor.

Like Monitor, Lock remembers its owning thread: Exit from another thread throws SynchronizationLockException, and await inside such a lock is forbidden by the same error CS1996.
cards/9/q: Write what the C# 13 compiler turns a lock on the new type into
cards/9/explain: EnterScope takes the lock and returns a Scope struct, and using guarantees its Dispose — leaving the lock — even on an exception. With a field of type object the compiler would generate Monitor.Enter/Exit.
cards/10/body:
• SemaphoreSlim — a user-mode counter. You know the main thing from the pitfalls unit: it has WaitAsync, and it is not tied to a thread.
  • ManualResetEventSlim — spins first, then waits through Monitor. It creates a real kernel event only if you ask for the WaitHandle property.
  • ReaderWriterLockSlim — many readers or one writer. There is an "upgradeable read" mode: you read and, if needed, upgrade the lock to a write. While a writer is waiting, new readers are held back — so the writer does not starve.

ReaderWriterLockSlim has its own cost for all that: tracking readers is more expensive than a plain lock. It wins only when reads vastly outnumber writes and each read takes noticeably longer than entering the lock.
cards/10/deep:
By default ReaderWriterLockSlim is created with LockRecursionPolicy.NoRecursion: re-entering on the same thread throws LockRecursionException. Only one thread at a time may hold an upgradeable read — otherwise two "upgrading" readers would wait for each other. The object is IDisposable.

The old ReaderWriterLock from .NET Framework 1.x is slower and has known problems — new code does not need it. All Slim primitives, like Monitor, work only inside one process.
cards/11/q: A reference data cache: 99% of calls are a 100 ns dictionary lookup, reloads are rare. What does replacing lock with ReaderWriterLockSlim give you?
cards/11/options/0: Most likely nothing, or a slowdown: tracking readers costs about as much as the read itself
cards/11/options/1: A speedup by the number of cores: readers do not get in each other's way
cards/11/options/2: A deadlock on the first reload
cards/11/options/3: Nothing changes: inside it is the same Monitor
cards/11/explain: Every reader entry is atomic operations on a shared counter, and its cache line bounces between cores just like with lock. With short reads there is no gain. Better here is an immutable snapshot of the data: readers take the reference without a lock, a reload swaps it via Volatile.Write or Interlocked.Exchange.
cards/12/q: Match the task with the primitive
cards/12/pairs/0/1: lock on a field of type Lock
cards/12/pairs/1/0: Wait for a condition under a lock
cards/12/pairs/4/0: One thread opens the gate for many
cards/13/options/0: A free lock is taken without entering the kernel
cards/13/options/1: Monitor.Wait can be called without holding the lock on that object
cards/13/options/2: A Lock cast to object behaves like Monitor in a lock statement
cards/13/options/3: SemaphoreSlim can be released from another thread
cards/13/explain: Wait without the lock throws SynchronizationLockException. Lock is mutual exclusion only, it has no condition variables. Casting to object throws away the whole point of the new type — that is what warning CS9216 is about.
